o: We are given a date string `YYYY-MM-DD` and must return which day of the year it is (1-indexed). For example, "2019-01-09" is simply day 9, while "2019-02-10" is 31 (January) + 10 = 41. The only subtlety is February's length, which depends on whether the year is a leap year. Since the input format is fixed and tiny, we just parse the three integers, sum the lengths of all months before the given month, add the day, and add 1 if the year is a leap year and the month is past February.
k: Parse the fixed-format string into year, month, day integers — no general date parsing needed.
A leap year is divisible by 4 but not by 100, unless also divisible by 400.
Only dates after February are affected by leap years; January/February need no adjustment.

a.n: Approach 1: Cumulative Month Days with Leap-Year Adjustment
a.i: Precompute the number of days in each month for a non-leap year: [31,28,31,30,31,30,31,31,30,31,30,31]. Sum the lengths of all months strictly before the target month, add the day of month, then add one extra day if the year is a leap year and the month index is greater than 2 (past February). This directly computes the answer without any iteration over days.
s: Split the string on '-' and parse year, month, day as integers.
Build an array of month lengths for a common year.
Sum month lengths for indices 0..month-2, then add day.
If the year is a leap year (divisible by 4 and not by 100, or divisible by 400) and month > 2, add 1.
a.t: O(1) — the string has fixed length 10 and the month loop runs at most 11 times.
a.sp: O(1) — only a constant-size array and a few integer variables.

a.i: Most languages can construct a date object from the parsed components and ask for its day-of-year directly (e.g., Python's `datetime` with a trick using two dates, or Java's `LocalDate.getDayOfYear()`). This avoids manual leap-year logic entirely and is the most robust choice in real code, though interviewers usually want the manual computation too.
s: Parse year, month, day from the string.
Construct a date object with those components.
Query the built-in day-of-year accessor and return it.
a.t: O(1) — constant work regardless of input.
a.sp: O(1) — a single date object per language runtime.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 since it demonstrates you understand leap-year rules and cumulative sums; mention the library approach as what you'd use in production code. Common pitfalls: forgetting the century rule (1900 is not a leap year even though divisible by 4 — relevant here since dates start at 1900!), applying the leap adjustment to January/February dates, and off-by-one errors when summing 'months before' vs 'months up to'. Edge cases worth testing: Jan 1 (day 1), Dec 31 of a leap year (day 366), Feb 29 itself, and 1900-03-01 (should be 60, not 61). Follow-ups might include computing the difference between two dates or handling arbitrary date formats.
